fields.title: Ostrov: Two Teams Arguing for Three Months
fields.summary: Retrospectives are happening, but nothing changes. Decide how to intervene.
fields.decisionPrompt: What will you do in this situation?
fields.brief/role: You are the PM for Ostrov.
fields.brief/company: Ostrov is a fictional online course platform for companies: 140 corporate clients, 60 thousand students.
fields.brief/context: The product is built by two teams: one is responsible for the platform and shared components, the other for what students see. For three months, every retrospective has ended in mutual complaints, and releases have slowed down significantly.
fields.brief/objective: Decide how to intervene in the situation.
fields.brief/constraints: You are the PM of the product team; the platform team reports to another manager. One quarter.
fields.brief/task: Choose what you will do and justify your decision.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: Team conflicts usually live in the queue, not in the people
fields.learnTakeaway/body: When two teams have been blaming each other for three months, the fastest move is to measure the handoff and show the numbers. Usually, it turns out that the actual work takes two days, while the wait time is sixteen, and the queue has no owner. Relationships mend themselves as soon as handoff rules, priorities, and recognition of one's own contribution are established.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
Time from decision to user: 31 days, compared to 12 six months ago.

Breakdown: product team work — 5 days; waiting for shared components from the platform team — 16 days; testing and release — 4 days; the rest is approvals.

Out of the last 20 product team tasks, 13 required changes in shared components.

The platform team has its own quarterly plan approved by their manager; the product team's requests are not included in it.

Work in progress (WIP): product team — 9 tasks for 6 people; platform team — 14 tasks for 7 people.

Over the quarter, the product team built workarounds in their code three times to avoid waiting. Two of the three later had to be rebuilt.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
Separate retrospectives, every two weeks.

In the product team, the refrain for three months has been: "the platform is blocking us."

In the platform team, according to their team lead: "the product team floods us with urgent requests without explanation."

No action items are recorded in either team.

There was one joint meeting: it ended with a list of mutual complaints, and they agreed to "communicate better."

The priority of product team requests to the platform team is not documented anywhere: whoever messages first gets in line.

The two managers have never discussed this issue with each other — both believe the problem lies with the other team.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
Requests are sent via messenger to specific platform team developers, whoever is available.

Out of 13 requests this quarter, 9 did not specify the deadline or the reason.

In 4 cases, a request was canceled after work had already started because the product team's priorities changed.

The platform team introduced a rule: requests are only accepted through their team lead. The product team considers this bureaucracy and continues to message developers directly.

Average request size — 2 days of work. Average wait time — 16 days.

One request — a shared SSO authorization component — is needed by three major clients and has been waiting for seven weeks.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
Three major clients are waiting for SSO; one of them wrote that if it's not delivered this quarter, they will consider another platform.

The Product Director is aware of the tension and suggests merging the teams into one.

The platform team manager feels his team is being used as a contractor.

Your manager suggests you "just talk to them and work it out like human beings."

Merging teams is a director-level decision, not yours.

Last quarter, they tried to keep a shared priority list in a spreadsheet; they stopped updating it after three weeks because no one was responsible for it.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Fix the handoff: queue, priority, and owner
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: Reduce the problem to what the measurement shows — 16 days of waiting at the handoff — agree on request handoff rules with a single queue owner, and escalate what is outside your authority.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
You bring numbers, not complaints, to the joint meeting: 16 out of 31 days is waiting at the handoff, 13 out of 20 tasks require shared components, the average request is 2 days of work with 16 days of waiting.
This changes the conversation: for the first time, the platform team sees they aren't being called a bottleneck out of spite.
You agree on three things: all requests go through their team lead with a deadline and reason, a single priority list with one owner (you), and a rule that a request canceled after starting is considered your mistake.
You put SSO first and explain why: three major clients, one ready to leave.
Separately, you escalate what is out of your hands: the platform team's plan doesn't account for product team requests, which is a decision for the two managers. You organize the meeting with them yourself.
Two months later, handoff wait time drops to 6 days, and no workarounds appear in the code.
Trade-off: the shared priority list requires your weekly time, and that is exactly why the previous spreadsheet died.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: People aren't listening to each other. Gather both teams and let them speak their minds to relieve tension.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
The meeting repeats the previous one: a list of complaints and an agreement to "communicate better."
No action items with an owner and deadline are recorded, so in two weeks everything goes back to how it was.
Requests continue to go directly via messenger, and priority is still determined by whoever writes first.
SSO is waiting for its ninth week; the major client repeats their warning in writing.
Trade-off: discussion is mistaken for a solution; however, the bulk of the problem is not in relationships, but in the lack of a queue and priority.
fields.decisionOptions/2/label: Stop depending on the platform team
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: Waiting 16 days is impossible. Build what is needed in your own code and stop asking for shared components.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
Speed indeed increases: the cycle time drops to 17 days in the very first month.
But two of the three previous workarounds already had to be rebuilt, and new ones suffer the same fate: authorization built separately diverges from the shared one and breaks during the next platform update.
SSO cannot be solved this way at all: it is a shared component by nature.
Relationships with the platform team deteriorate, and their manager completely stops accounting for your requests in their plan.
Trade-off: local speed is bought at the cost of technical debt that will return, and a complete breakdown of the handoff that will still have to be fixed.
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: The Product Director suggested this himself. Escalate the issue and remove the boundary between the teams.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
You raise the issue, and this is the right level: platform team plans are indeed not decided by you.
But merging is a heavy organizational change: the discussion takes six weeks, during which nothing changes.
SSO waits all this time.
Eventually, the teams are merged, and a quarter later speed recovers — though some platform tasks for other products are left without an owner.
Trade-off: the heaviest tool was chosen instead of the cheapest; request handoff rules could have been introduced in a week without waiting for a reorganization.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: No measurement of where work is stuck: waiting is not separated from active work
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Process discussions do not end with an action item that has an owner and a deadline
